t-6.3-network-diagrams.title: 6.3 Sequence Activities (continued): lags, network diagrams, path convergence and divergence
t-6.3-network-diagrams.notes: Lag = time a successor is delayed relative to its predecessor (editing starts 15 days after writing starts = SS with 15-day lag). Network diagrams show lags as e.g. SS+10 even without a timescale. The team decides which dependencies need leads or lags; leads and lags must not replace schedule logic; duration estimates never include leads or lags; document activities and assumptions. PMIS scheduling software sequences activities, inserts relationships, leads and lags, and distinguishes dependency types. Output: project schedule network diagram - graphical representation of logical relationships (dependencies), manual or software-produced, detailed or with summary activities, often with a narrative explaining unusual sequences. Path convergence = an activity with multiple predecessors; path divergence = an activity with multiple successors; both carry greater risk. Figure 6-11 (visually verified) example: Begin feeds A, H and K; A->B; B->C is SS; C->D->E; B->E; H->C; H->F; F->G is FS+15; H->I is SS+10; K->I; K->L; I->J; L->J is FF; E, G and J feed End. Activity I is a convergence (H and K); K is a divergence (I and L). Document updates: activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, milestone list.

t-6.4-estimate-durations.title: 6.4 Estimate Activity Durations: effort vs duration factors, analogous, parametric, three-point, bottom-up, reserves
t-6.4-estimate-durations.notes: Estimate the number of work periods needed for each activity with estimated resources; key benefit: how long each activity takes; performed throughout. Uses scope of work, resource types/skills, quantities and resource calendars; also constraints (fixed duration, fixed effort, fixed number of resources) and the network analysis technique. Inputs come from the people most familiar with the work; estimates are progressively elaborated as data improves. Estimates effort and available resources, then converts to work periods using project and resource calendars; changing a driving resource usually changes duration, but not linearly; some work takes a fixed time regardless (24-hour stress test). Factors: law of diminishing returns; number of resources (doubling people rarely halves time - risk, knowledge transfer, learning curve, coordination); advances in technology; staff motivation - Student Syndrome (procrastination until the deadline) and Parkinson's Law (work expands to fill the time available). Document all data and assumptions. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, accuracy); scope baseline (WBS dictionary technical details); documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, lessons learned, milestone list, project team assignments, RBS, resource calendars, resource requirements - lower-skilled or extra resources may lengthen duration via communication/training/coordination, risk register); EEFs (duration estimating databases, productivity metrics, published commercial information, team location); OPAs (historical durations, project calendars, estimating policies, scheduling methodology, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment; analogous estimating (uses actual values - duration, budget, size, weight, complexity - of a similar past activity/project; gross value, adjusted for known differences; used when detail is limited; cheaper and quicker but less accurate; most reliable when past work is similar in fact, not just appearance, and estimators have expertise); parametric estimating (algorithm/statistical relationship between historical data and variables, e.g., quantity x labour hours per unit: 1,000 m of cable at 25 m/hour = 40 hours; accuracy depends on the model); three-point estimating (most likely tM, optimistic tO, pessimistic tP; triangular distribution tE = (tO + tM + tP) / 3 used with insufficient history or judgmental data; gives expected duration and range of uncertainty. NOTE: the Guide states only the triangular formula in 6.4; the beta distribution formula (cO + 4cM + cP) / 6 is stated in Cost 7.2.2.5 (PDF 282, confirmed in batch B12), so lessons present beta for durations as the same weighting applied to tO, tM, tP and cite 7.2.2.5); bottom-up estimating (decompose an activity that cannot be estimated confidently and aggregate the detailed estimates; document resource dependencies); data analysis - alternatives analysis (resource capability/skill levels, compression techniques, manual vs automated tools, make/rent/buy) and reserve analysis (contingency reserve = schedule reserve inside the schedule baseline for identified, accepted risks - known-unknowns; may be a % of duration or fixed work periods; may be aggregated; used, reduced or removed as information improves; clearly identified. Management reserve = withheld for management control for unforeseen in-scope work - unknown-unknowns; not in the schedule baseline but part of overall duration requirements; using it may require a baseline change depending on contract terms); decision making - voting incl. fist of five (closed fist = no support to five fingers = full support; anyone showing fewer than three fingers discusses objections; repeat until everyone shows three or more or the team moves on); meetings - in agile, sprint/iteration planning on the first day with product owner, Scrum team and PM: discuss prioritised backlog items, commit, break stories into tasks estimated in hours, validate against capacity; outputs iteration backlog, assumptions, concerns, risks, dependencies, decisions, actions. Outputs: duration estimates (quantitative assessments of likely work periods; exclude lags; may show a range - '2 weeks +/- 2 days' = 8 to 12 days on a 5-day week - or a probability - '15% probability of exceeding 3 weeks' = 85% probability of 3 weeks or less); basis of estimates (how derived, assumptions, constraints, range such as +/-10%, confidence level, individual risks); document updates (activity attributes, assumption log, lessons learned).

t-6.5-develop-schedule.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule: inputs, schedule network analysis, critical path method, float
t-6.5-develop-schedule.notes: Analyse activity sequences, durations, resource requirements and schedule constraints to create the schedule model; key benefit: a model with planned dates; performed throughout. Iterative: may revise duration, resource estimates and schedule reserves to reach an approved schedule that becomes the baseline. Key steps: define milestones, identify and sequence activities, estimate durations; then assigned staff review their dates against resource calendars and other commitments; analyse logic conflicts and need for resource leveling before approval and baselining; maintain a realistic model throughout. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, tool, how calculated); scope baseline; documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, basis of estimates, duration estimates, lessons learned, milestone list, network diagrams, project team assignments, resource calendars, resource requirements, risk register - schedule-relevant risk reflected in schedule reserves using expected/mean impact); agreements (vendors' input on how they will meet commitments); EEFs (standards, communication channels); OPAs (scheduling methodology, project calendars). Schedule network analysis: the overarching technique generating the schedule model, using CPM, resource optimisation and modelling; also assess whether to aggregate schedule reserves where paths converge or diverge, and review whether the critical path has high-risk or long-lead items needing reserves or risk responses; iterate until viable. Critical path method: estimates minimum project duration and schedule flexibility; computes early start (ES), early finish (EF), late start (LS) and late finish (LF) by forward and backward pass, ignoring resource limits. Critical path = sequence of activities forming the longest path through the project, which determines the shortest possible project duration; it has the least total float, usually zero. Early/late dates are not the schedule itself but windows in which activities could occur. Total float = how long an activity can be delayed or extended from its early start without delaying the project finish or violating a constraint. Critical paths may have positive, zero or negative total float depending on constraints: positive when the backward pass starts from a constraint later than the forward-pass early finish; negative when a late-date constraint is violated by duration and logic; negative float analysis finds ways to accelerate a delayed schedule. Networks may have near-critical paths. To get zero or positive float, adjust durations (more resources or less scope), discretionary logic, leads and lags or constraints. Free float = how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor or violating a constraint. Figure 6-16 (visually verified; day-1 convention, i.e., EF = ES + duration - 1 and the successor's ES = predecessor's EF + 1): A (ES1, dur 5, EF5; LS1, TF0, LF5); B (6, 5, 10; 11, TF5, 15); C (6, 10, 15; 6, 0, 15); D (16, 15, 30; 16, 0, 30). Path A-B-D = 25, path A-C-D = 30 = critical path. Free float of B = 5 days.

t-6.5-optimisation-compression.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule (continued): resource leveling vs smoothing, what-if, Monte Carlo, crashing vs fast tracking
t-6.5-optimisation-compression.notes: Resource optimisation adjusts start/finish dates so planned resource use is at or below availability. Resource leveling: adjusts dates based on resource constraints to balance demand with supply - used when shared or critical resources are available only at certain times or in limited quantities, are over-allocated (Figure 6-17: Sue assigned 16 hours on one day across A and B; after leveling her work spreads over two days), or to keep usage constant; uses available float and can change (often lengthen) the critical path. Resource smoothing: keeps resource requirements within predefined limits without changing the critical path or delaying completion - activities move only within free and total float; may not optimise all resources. Data analysis: what-if scenario analysis ('what if scenario X happens?' - e.g., late component delivery, longer engineering, strike, permit changes - computed on the schedule to test feasibility and prepare reserves and response plans); simulation (models combined effects of individual risks and other uncertainty; most common is Monte Carlo analysis, which calculates possible project outcomes from probability distributions; Figure 6-18: 10% probability of finishing by the 13 May target, 90% by 28 May). Leads and lags are refinements used in limited circumstances during network analysis. Schedule compression shortens duration without reducing scope to meet constraints, imposed dates or objectives; negative float analysis helps. Crashing: shorten duration for the least incremental cost by adding resources (overtime, extra resources, paying to expedite) - only works on critical path activities where more resources actually shorten duration; may increase risk and/or cost. Fast tracking: activities or phases normally done in sequence are done in parallel for at least part of their duration (e.g., foundation before all architectural drawings are complete) - may cause rework, increase risk and possibly cost; only works where activities can overlap on the critical path; using leads increases coordination effort and quality risk. Figure 6-19 compares normal, crashing (higher cost) and fast tracking (higher risk). (Continued on PDF 253.)
